narrative:
The model predicts you have a 12% chance of failing your final year. While this is a relatively low probability, the system flags it as enough of a risk that you are required to take remedial courses to strengthen your preparation.

The prediction that you might fail is driven mainly by three aspects of your situation. The most influential factor is that you have had no past class failures. Surprisingly, this actually pushes the model toward expecting you to fail. Among students who passed, having zero previous failures is the average, yet in your specific combination of circumstances the model interprets this clean record as indicating you may lack the resilience that comes from having overcome earlier setbacks.

The second most important influence is your weekly study time of more than ten hours. This is far above what most successful students report (only 3.4% of passers study this much), but the model sees it as pushing slightly toward failure. It appears the system believes such intense last-minute cramming may not be as effective as steadier, moderate study habits.

Finally, the fact that you receive extra educational support at school also contributes to the prediction of possible failure. Very few students who ultimately pass (only 3.4%) get this support, so the model treats it as a warning sign that you may be starting from a weaker position than your peers.

To improve, consider shifting from long study marathons to more consistent daily work, building small challenges that help you develop resilience, and discussing with your teachers whether the extra support can be refocused on proactive skill-building rather than catch-up. These small changes can meaningfully raise your chances of passing.
